utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is given to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before we start, I think that the court officer has distributed the report to the Bench and to my learned friends. In order to follow this testimony, I would like to ask my colleague here to distribute this document about footnotes so that everybody can follow easier. The testimony and the footnotes refer to the exhibits -- to documents that we are going to tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you so kind to state your full name and last name, year of birth, and your occupation?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am Colonel Bozidar Forca, an active-duty serviceman in the army of Serbia. That is to say, I am currently serving as deputy chief of administration for development of the army of Serbia General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I also asked you to give us the year of birth, place of birth. And then please slowly tell us about your educational background as well as your career details, the offices you held individually, and what have you done in your academic work so far?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: I was born on the 8th of January, 1957, in the village of Brovac, the municipality of Backa Palanka, which is located in Serbia in the province of Vojvodina. I completed elementary school in that village and I completed my secondary school in Backa Palanka. Following the secondary school, where I received military scholarship throughout four years, I enrolled in the military academy in Belgrade in the infantry department. The education was first conceived in such a way at that time that the first three years of schooling took place in Belgrade and the last fourth year was attended in Sarajevo in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I completed military academy, the infantry department in 1979, and I was appointed to my first post in the centre of military technical schools of ground forces in Zagreb. This is the centre that mostly educated and trained officers and other military personnel for technical specialties, logistical specialties and so on. As an infantry man, I was appointed commander of a platoon of cadets attending the military academy, and I served in that post until 1985. Given that I was trained as an infantry man, we, from various branches of service were sent to attend training for teachers and then they selected teachers among us. So that from the rank of lieutenant, I also was appointed as a teacher. I taught tactics. I taught at the military secondary school level, and I also taught at the military academy level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Certainly. I always said -- or, rather, it was always said that I served as an example of a leader among teachers. What does this mean? This means that as soon as I started teaching, I was sent to the Zagreb university where I completed a training course for young teachers which lasted for four months. As I developed as a teacher, I was sent to the school centre in Sarajevo where I completed a course for commanders of infantry battalions which lasted five months. Following that, I passed exams for the rank of major which was a condition to be appointed to a higher function at the time. In the military academy in 1985 when my year graduated, I remained within that same military academy, and I was appointed to the department of military education where I served as a teacher of tactics. When I retired --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, could you slow down even more.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Certainly. When I retired -- or, rather, when the colonel who taught command and control subjects retired, I was appointed teacher of command and control and I served in that post until the centre was relocated from Zagreb to Belgrade in 1991 due to the well-known wartime events in Croatia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the operations in Vukovar in 1991, where were you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: In 1991, as the Vukovar operation was in progress, I was under the siege in the centre of military and technical schools. The siege was laid by the Croatian paramilitary forces, and the siege meant that we were unable to leave the barracks. Water and electricity supply had been cut off, they fired at us, they launched grenades and bombs at us, and they insulted us on ethnical grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where was the centre?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: It was in Zagreb in Crnomerec municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Now, would you please be so kind and describe the rest of your military and professional career but in less detail, please. You have to follow the words on the transcript in front of you, otherwise not everything you say will be recorded.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Upon my arrival in Belgrade in December of 1991, I remained at the military technical academy which had been relocated to Belgrade. I remained there until September of 1992 when I was transferred to the institute of war skills, which is an academic facility now called military research institute. There, in that institute, I had to focus on my own professional and academic advancement, and to that end I completed my masters studies in 1994. I acquired a Ph.D degree in 2003. This is as far as the academic advancement is concerned, as it is known in our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down. Please follow the transcript and when you see that the typing has stopped, then you may proceed. I'm sure that you are nervous a little bit, but with time it is bound to get better.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: As I said, within my academic advancement, I completed my masters degree and acquired a Ph.D degree. As for my professional advanced learning, there were several trainings. There was a command staff school and the school of national defence, which were the highest learning facilities within our army. In 1997, I also graduated from the school of national defence. Thus, within my professional advancement, I have achieved the maximum, if one may say so. I hold a Ph.D degree in military science, and I am also a graduate of the school of national defence. Naturally, this is not the end of it. In addition to that, I was sent to England, to York, to further my knowledge of the English language. I visited many countries of Europe where I attended various advanced learning courses. I went to Zagreb to RACVIAC centre, where we dealt with regional arms control. Then I went to Madrid, to Spain, which was sponsored by the Human Rights Commissioner for European Union, or Council of Europe, and owing to the donation of the Ministry of Defence of Italy, I completed the first degree studies of the Italian language. I also attended a school of -- NATO school in Oberammergau in Germany where I attended some courses. I also travelled professionally to Bulgaria, to the United States, and I also met with various foreign military dignitaries when they visited our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Forca. The report that you drafted has two parts. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does the first part pertain to the doctrinal and legal provisions of the armed forces of the SFRY and is it focused on command and control system from brigade to squad?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: This first part of your report, does it have two subparts and can you tell us something about them? We will first cover the table of contents and then we will proceed to individual questions. Is the first subpart dealing with tasks, organisation, recruitment, and replenishment of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And then within the second subpart, you deal with command and control of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The second part of your report once again has two subparts; the first subpart is previous operations, and the second subpart is Guards Motorised Brigade, Operations Group South in Operation Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you to turn to the questions pertaining to the first part of your report, which is the part dealing with command and control of the armed forces, and this will serve as an introduction into what we will need further on from your analysis. My first question, Professor: Briefly can you explain to us the relationship between the -- such terms as command and control in the armed forces of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, in our theory and practice, as well as in the theory and practice of the period that we are dealing with, there was a dilemma and there was a disagreement, there was a lack of full consensus on the relationship between the terms "command and control." In that sense, I stated in my report that in different rules and regulations, this notion was given different names. As a result of that, as one of the sources which was respected a great deal in the armed forces of the SFRY, there was a book called "Some Issues and Problems in the Command and Control of Armed Forces." That was the source that I referred to. Essentially, during that period of time - I must stress this - one of the leading theoretician of the theory of command and control in the armed forces of the SFRY was Dr. Branislav Jovanovic, a colonel at the time. In his observation of command and control, he most frequently spoke of two options or directions. The first one was that the notions of command and control were actually synonyms, that they had the same meaning. The second option was that the control was a broader notion or concept than command and that command and control entailed planning, organising, command, coordination, and control or inspection. Bearing in mind the rules that are known to you, and bearing in mind the relationship between theory and practice, the person who is in command may be said that he is the one deciding on the use of the unit, that he issues orders, and conducts the inspection. In the process, the other functions in that same field, they constitute command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Forca. Here is the second question. Can you tell us what the difference is between the notions of principles and factors of command and control? Because of course we want to hear your opinion, as opposed to the opinion of some other expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Of course. Your Honours, you will know that I was present here in the courtroom when Prosecution expert witnesses testified, and this issue of the relationship between the principle, on the one hand, and the factor on the other was raised. In my view, General Pringle, who was the expert witness for the Prosecution, confused the provisions relating to the principles and factors. Now, why do I say this? Because in our theory, and before this Tribunal there is the exhibit, the manual on command and control for military academies, there is a clear distinction between the control principles and control factors. You see, in our theory there existed alongside the notions of principles that were referred to in the B/C/S in two different ways, "nacela" and "principi." But what is the difference now between the notion of principle if it's taken from the legislation on the unity of command, continuity of command, flexibility and so on and so forth, and factors on the other side? It stems from the practice and experience a priori and a posteriori. The principles govern the rules according to which the soldiers have to behave in combat. It doesn't really matter whether a theory arises from experience or from theoretical or empirical aspects. The principles have to be valid both before and after combat operations, and then it is possible to say that. If it was not the case that the principles were adhered to, one could say that this is the case of deviating from the standard practice. The principles always fit into the circumstances of a given case. Specifically, in order for an event to take place, certain conditions have to be put in place. They can be either sufficient, necessary, or active factors. In the point where these three groups of conditions overlap, the causes of a certain event can be established. When we speak of certain social events, such as an armed combat or an armed operation, in these social events, there exists the factor which is called an awareness of the objective. Therefore, the factors, unlike the principles, are the determinants of a specific situation, and they are clearly stated in the manual on command and control of the academy, and they consist in objectives, discipline, processes, responsibilities and so on and so forth. And with all due respect, I had to say that Mr. Pringle did confuse the principles and factors, because when talking about the principles he mentioned the discipline and responsibility and so on and so forth which, in fact, are factors rather than principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On the matter of control and command, specifically on the climate of command, can you tell us which factors impacted on the climate of command in the Vukovar operation?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will once again have to refer to my learned colleague Mr. Pringle. When talking of the climate of command in his report, Mr. Pringle specifically talked of the commander, or komandir, as being relevant. This isn't in fact inaccurate but is incomplete. When we speak of the climate of command in a given operation, namely the Operation Vukovar, we cannot overlook the influence of the commander but this is taken into account only as a third step. Now why? The climate of command, in a given operation, is subject to different influences, factors, and I defined them a moment ago, and they can be categorised as general and specific: The break-up of the country, civil war as perhaps the most difficult form of war. The decision that the reserve forces should be used for up to 45 days, and all the other conditions were the ones who overrule or carry more weight than the commander himself, regardless of the commander's qualifications, knowledge, authority, and the extent to which he adhered to the other principles. Therefore, in connection with this, I conclude that it wasn't only up to the commander, or komandir, to define what sort of climate command will have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Forca, can you tell us what the following terms mean: Resubordination, attaching, and finally, the notion of coordinated action or coordination; and, technically speaking, what is the difference between these different terms?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Certainly. Your Honour, I have to say that these terms, just as the other terms of military skills are part of military theory. I decided to highlight certain differences existing between these terms, and they are quite evident, in order to clarify the position and actions of the commanders and units involved in the Vukovar operation. When we say "resubordination," what we mean to say is that the commander, or the komandir, detaches from his establishment formation elements of a certain unit and resubordinates them to the commander of another unit. For example, the commander of the Guards Brigade in his first decision dated the 1st of October, 1991, detached one platoon from the military police battalion and resubordinated it to the commander of the 1st Battalion or, rather, to the commander of the element of the combat disposition, which was called the 1st Assault Detachment. Every unit in times of peace and war has its well defined establishment. Detaching elements of units from an establishment formation and resubordination to another commander is called resubordination. In a specific situation where in a certain area of combat operations several units are present which are active under the command of a single commander but which do not belong to the same establishment formation, such as, for instance, Operations Group South, this was not an establishment formation. An establishment formation is the Guards Brigade. When one of these units -- or, rather, when the commander detaches from one of these units its assets such as tanks, vehicles, and so on and so forth to another unit, then this constitutes attaching. When units involved in combat have a clearly defined task and the objective that they are to achieve, as well as the area in which they are to be active, and they also have a neighbour in front, to the right, left, and back, their joint action is called "coordination." Units that act in coordination are not in a relationship of subordination. Not one of them is superior or subordinate to any of the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You explained to us the notion of resubordination. You can refer to specific example, of course. Can you remember any example of attaching or coordinated action in the Vukovar operation? You can refer to this now or at a later stage, but at any rate it would be good that in testifying you refer to specific examples.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Well, I hope I will have enough time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I do believe that this would be very helpful for the Bench. But you can do this at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Of course, yes, I will find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, you can do that later. I just wanted to let you know that it would be very helpful to us in the courtroom if you are specific. Can you tell us what the difference is and what the definition is of the command post and observation post?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in addition to the obvious linguistic difference in terms of the title, there are substantial differences in terms of meaning. Both the command post and observation post serve for the purposes of command and control in the preparation stage and combat stage. The command post is set up by units which have the command at the time and these are units from the strength of battalion and above. Specifically speaking, battalion and a brigade. A command post is located on a given area which is proportionate to the size of the units. It may cover features, and I mean fixed features such as buildings or built features, or fortifications, temporary features such as tents, and motor vehicles. In higher level units, there are several types of command posts, such as the main command post, the rear command post, alternate command post, or reserve command post, and, for the purposes of camouflage, there is also the so-called decoy command post. The observation post of the komandir, commander, therefore the observation post of the komandir and not the command, is set up and organised by the units of the strength of company, platoon, and squad. Just as was the case with the command post, the observation post can be housed in a building or in the open area, in a fortification, and it is set up by the commander, komandir, and he uses the post to command combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Forca, the duty of a company commander was considered to be one of the most difficult positions in the JNA; is that right? Do you agree with that? If so, why?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I would put it this way, Your Honours. There was no law stating that this was the most difficult post. It was a general truth among us officers. This was a maxim that was tried and true. Why? Everything done by a commander and his assistants within a command, that is members of the command as a totality, is done by the commander alone at company level. For a while in the JNA, even a company officer, company NCOs were abolished so that the commander at the time had to take care of everything in the unit, the replenishment, their life and work, all the conditions, the equipment, as well as the security of his unit. All these different jobs are performed by special bodies in a command. An infantry company at the time numbered about 150 men, including all their equipment. What it took was to know each of the commanders, each of the soldiers, and to look after all of them was an exceptionally difficult duty and most officers considered this to be the most difficult stage in their military career.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, at the time, what was the make-up of the personnel in the Guards Brigade and by that I mean both officers and ordinary soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, this specific answer is also contained in my report. I do wish to point out the following: When talking about the factor of personnel, of manpower, officers, NCOs and civilians, as well as ordinary soldiers involved, the Guards Brigade was a top-notch unit of the JNA. You might even call it an elite unit. Just to digress a little, in any country where you have a guard-like unit such as the Guards Brigade, and I have had occasion to see for myself that this was indeed the case, invariably this unit involves top-notch officers, elite officers, and NCOs. As for ordinary soldiers and replenishment, recruitment officers -- or, rather, military officers were obliged to send top-class, top-notch soldiers only to a unit that was the equivalent of a Guards Brigade. As for NCOs and civilians, these normally had to be highly qualified NCOs and very successful ones who enjoyed a high degree of respect in their military environment but also in their civilian environment. These are to be men, if I may put it this way, who, under no circumstances, were allowed to have any sort of criminal record at all. One took a lot of pride and all of us soldiers know that in serving in the Guards Brigade. It was a great honour. And that was the view we held of any officers or NCOs from the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, can you now please explain the relation between the temporary forces of operations group and the tactical group, on the one hand, and the assault detachment, or JOD, and assault groups on the other?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as theory goes, there are the definitions and there is the defining of these concepts mentioned by Mr. Borovic. You can find it in dictionaries, you can find it in the encyclopedia, which are the most general theoretical sources available, but you can also find these in the rules governing the work of JNA units. Any units in which these formations could, in theory, have been established. What do all these share, operations group, the tactical group, the assault detachment, and the assault groups? What they all share is that these are temporary formations. What is the distinction exactly? There is a distinction. I would like to say that the distinction has not been clarified to a sufficient extent the last time I was here when Mr. Theunens and Mr. Pringle testified about these subjects. We have an operations group and we have a tactical group. There is a difference in level between these two. However, they are both formations, functional formations or organisational formations, which means that they comprise the establishment's units or establishment units. When whoever is charge of taking decisions decides that an establishment unit such as, for example, the Guards Brigade cannot possibly carry out a task on its own, it is then that this person enlists the assistance of other establishment units for the purposes of this task. For example, in Vukovar, you had the 80th [Realtime transcript read in error "18th"] Motorised Brigade, the 20th Partisan Brigade, and other establishment units coming in to assist. Tactical group and the operations group are somewhat more than the Guards Brigade but fall short of being the corps, because the corps is an operations formation, and that's why it was called an operations group, because it comprised establishment units. The assault detachment and the assault group are also establishment units but they are mere elements of a combat disposition. Now what does that mean? What this means is, for example, the commander of the operations group, I'm talking about the structural organisation such as battalions, divisions, and detachments, the commander takes a decision to make a functional organisation and then this is the combat disposition. The elements of this combat disposition, or combat order, because actually both terms were used, are not the same as establishment units. For example, in the establishment of the Guards Brigade, there was several battalions, the motorised Battalion, the armoured battalion, but when we introduce the elements of combat disposition, then you say, for example, offensive forces. Since the attack is on a built-up area, and this is what the rules dictate, one must set up an assault detachment and an assault group as elements of the disposition. They perform this task until the task is completed, and then pending further decisions they can be sent back to their original unit. These two must be distinguished regardless of the fact that they are both temporary formations. The operations and tactical group on the one hand, and the assault detachment and group on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: There is an error in the transcript, Your Honours. The transcript says the 18th Motorised Brigade as an example cited by Mr. Forca. It should be the 80th Motorised Brigade but we all know that by now. This is at line 16 -- page 16 line 2, rather. Thank you. Mr. Forca, which unit could have been given the role of an assault group within the brigade's battalion, which unit could have been appointed to perform that role?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, when we talk about an assault group at brigade level as envisaged by the rules for brigades, it is possible to set up assault detachments. If you have a battalion, assault detachments can be set up within the combat disposition as well as assault groups, and according to these rules for battalions, they normally have the strength of a reinforced platoon. If we look at the provisions of the rules for platoons and companies, there is explicit reference there to the company as a possible element of combat disposition within the brigade but of the assault detachment, which means an assault group normally has the strength of up to a reinforced platoon. In the rules there is no reference to the company as an assault group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's fine. How can one reinforce a company in combat? If you could perhaps refer to a specific example, and please continue slowly, carry on with this subject. Pages 11 and 12. I think there are references to that at pages 11 and 12.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, we talked about the concepts of resubordination and attachment. And we said that these two constituted jointly reinforcement of a unit to which another element had been subordinated or attached. In terms of principle, and in terms of the rules, any unit can be reinforced by a lower-level unit. Specifically, when looking at an infantry company involved in fighting, and this is also in the company and platoon rules, that's 11/12, item 4, in order to carry out a combat task, a company can be reinforced by a platoon of recoilless -- of 82-millimetre recoilless cannon, an 82-millimetre mortar platoon, and in exceptional circumstances, by a mortar battery 120-millimetre, a guns battery, a platoon of pioneers or tanks or ABHO scouts. Under special circumstances, it can also be reinforced by a TO platoon. That's what the company platoon rules say. A company can be reinforced by using lower-level units, lower-level in relation to its own level. That's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Forca, having said this, can you please answer a very important question: What is the relation between the responsibility of a commander, or komandir, on the one hand, and command responsibility on the other? Can you please explain this as closely as possible to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: I'll do my best. Your Honours, this appears to be a mere pun, the responsibility of a commander, or komandir, on the one hand, and command responsibility on the other. However, both in terms of rules and in terms of practice, I, and I believe I'm right on this one, draw a distinction between these two concepts. First of all, all JNA commands, all commanders and all komandirs had their duties and competencies clearly defined. They were responsible for the overall situation in their own units, which means for life and work in their units. In this sense, it meant the carrying out of combat missions as part of combat operations performed by their units. This is the responsibility of the commander or komandir. As a factor -- earlier we spoke about the factors affecting command and control. This is assessed in relation to each new situation arising. On the other hand, command responsibility as a concept did not exist in our military science at the time or indeed in our military practice. However, the concept of responsibility for acts committed by subordinates is something that did exist, and this is explicitly stated in item 21 of the rules on the application of the international law of war and its provisions. I'm not sure if there is any need to go into that and read out parts of it now, but that item says: "Responsibility for acts committed by one's subordinate: A military officer is personally responsible for any infractions of the law of war. In as far as he knew or had reason to know that any of his subordinates or other units and individuals were preparing to commit any such violations at the time when it was possible to prevent these violations, he failed to take appropriate pressures to stop them." Also, an officer who knows that violations of the law of war were committed is personally responsible if he fails to take legal action against the perpetrators or unless it is not within his remit if it is -- if it is not within his remit to take legal steps, he should at least report this officer to his superior. That's the first thing. And the next thing in that item is: "A military officer is responsible as a co-perpetrator or instigator if, by failing to take measures against those subordinates in violation of the law of -- the provisions of the law of war, he contributed to his subordinates, units or individuals committing other such violations." That's it. The term we mentioned, "responsibility for acts committed by one's subordinates" is here defined as command responsibility, and it specifies here to which persons that refers, as opposed to the responsibility of a commander for the overall life and work, so to speak, of his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, I think that we can turn now to part 2, which has two subparts. Again, we don't need to repeat what is stated in your report. Can we now turn to the portion entitled -- to the part that is entitled "Previous operations." I think it would be useful if you were to tell us, based on the entire literature that you had available or that you studied whether you were able to establish what were the tasks of the JNA in combat operations in Vukovar and in Croatia itself back in 1991, and then we can turn to Vukovar itself.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honour, as for the tasks that the Yugoslav Peoples' Army had in the fall of 1991, there are documents to that effect, the documents of the highest military leadership. And by your leave, in reply to this question of Mr. Borovic, I would like to mention the statement given by the deputy federal secretary for national defence given at the session for national defence board or committee on the 6th of November, 1991, where he gave two key tasks. The first one was to protect the Serbian population, and the second one was to lift the siege or blockade of the garrison. These facts can be found in the document entitled "collection of documents regarding defence and security of Yugoslavia 1990 to 1991." This was published and all of these documents can be found in this collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever find out who ordered the attack on Vukovar in the military sense?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer to this question has an implicit and an explicit aspect. An implicit aspect is that the statement given by the late General Panic are well-known. He gave them in his interview as he was explaining the significance of Vukovar. In that regard, they are implicit, or it was implicitly stated that the attack and the liberation of Vukovar came as a result of the decision taken by the commander of the 1st Military District. If this can be seen as a general aspect, we should also look at the more particular aspect, and that can be gleaned from the order given by the commander of the 1st Guards Brigade on the 1st of October. Although I personally did not see that document -- I'm not referring to the order of the commander of the Guards Brigade, but the other one, namely that the commander of the Operations Group South at the time when that post was not occupied by the commander of the Guards Brigade issued an order to attack. The document that was available to me at that level was the document of the commander of the Guards Brigade dated the 1st of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who served as commander of the Operation Group South at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Would you please specify the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The 1st of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on available data and the war log books, the commander of the Operations Group South was Colonel Bajo Bojat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about after that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: I don't have the document -- or, rather, it wasn't available to me, the document specifying that the post of the commander of the Operations Group South was taken over by Colonel Mrksic who is a retired general now. However, based on the inspection of the war log which mentions the date of the 8th of October, 1991, one can conclude that Colonel Mrksic took over the post of the commander of the Operations Group South from Colonel Bojat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But you remain to your previous statement that you did not see the document about the handover of duty?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that document. It wasn't available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: We heard you refer to Serbian and Croatian population in Vukovar. Would you please tell us: In addition to there being Serbian population, why else Vukovar was supposed to be liberated?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I have already stated, there is a barracks in Vukovar where there were members of the JNA who had come under the attack of Croatian paramilitary forces. I was one of such people who found themselves in a besieged barracks and there were many such barracks. I quoted to you the statement given by the deputy federal secretary of national defence, and I told you about the tasks that they gave. The second one was to lift the siege of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was referring to the first bit; namely, that they needed to save both the Serbian and Croatian population who were besieged by Croatian paramilitary forces. Was that also the task?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That was not the testimony. And that's a leading question. That was not the testimony that he gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I don't mind if they ask him what the first objective was but not do it leadingly, especially where it's not according to his testimony, previous testimony, or his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You see the issue, Mr. Borovic? Would you like to rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, you quoted the words of General Kadijevic, and based on the entire documentation that you analysed in your capacity of an expert, in addition to the lifting of the siege of the barracks, what were the other goals of liberating Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: I quoted to you the two tasks that were specified, and in response to your question, I can reply that it is a well-known fact that in the shelters, basements, refugee groups, there were citizens of the city of Vukovar. And that could have been the objective, too, to free those citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you please turn to your expert report, and let us now turn to its part 2, which I believe is the most important one for us here. It deals with the Guards Motorised Brigade; that is to say, with the Operations Group South in the Vukovar operation. I'm going to put some questions to you that mostly concern my client and the 3rd Company that was under his command. The commander of the 3rd Company, that is to say, Miroslav Radic, was he able to effect the mission of going to Vukovar? Was he able to effect it in any way?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, the answer is no. Because for an operation of that complexity the decision is made and the mission is defined by command at a much higher level. So my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question: Upon being sent to Vukovar, was the commander of the 3rd Company in the position to effect the composition or make-up of his company?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Once again, my answer is in the negative because it is well-known how the units of the JNA are staffed. The task of the company commander in that respect was to assign these soldiers with different military specialties to different establishment posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned this military specialty. Is it also known under the acronym VES?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes, it is known as VES.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 3rd Motorised Company, Captain Radic, did he effect in any way the objective of the attack on Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, once again, when it comes to the attack on Vukovar, my answer is in the negative yet again. As I said previously, the decision to attack Vukovar is not taken at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: At which level is it taken?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: It is taken at the operations and strategic level, only at that level could such a decision be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And to reduce it to the terms that we are familiar with, tell us what commander could have made that decision?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: If we go from top to bottom, which is the logic of the chain of command, that decision could have been taken by the commander of the 1st Military District who would have conveyed it to the Operations Group South, and then the one that he would be conveying this to the commander of the Guards Brigade. And then we have a document detailing how that was conveyed further down to his subordinates. Only the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion or his deputy could have issued an order to the 3rd Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the commander of the 3rd Motorised Company, could he have effected the replenishment and reinforcement of his unit?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Well, the answer is both yes and no. How come yes and no? As we have said already, that bringing up the unit to the establishment strength is a matter which is regulated. Troops are sent to the commander of a unit for certain purposes, so to that extent, the answer is yes. It is yes in the sense that there can be certain events in the course of combat. For example, people could be killed, wounded, or the numbers of troops could be reduced for whatever reason. Based on that, the company commander is authorised to turn to his superior through regular channels, asking for additional men, or in view of a specific mission, he can ask for additional reinforcement. That doesn't mean that he will necessarily get what he asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Forca. Now, will you please assist us and briefly describe the procedure in adopting and implementing a decision in combat operations in Vukovar two levels above and two levels below the level of a company commander? I believe this is quite important for us.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Very well. The principle of two levels above and two levels below is not the principle that exists only in the JNA, no, it is present in the armed forces of other countries as well. It is important to have knowledge of it in order to find out the answer as to how a company commander was given a task in any particular case and how he conveyed this task to his subordinates. Your Honours, in that sense, as we analyse brigades, since a brigade is exactly two levels above a company, in our theory and practice, there are documents concerning command and control which describe this in great detail. One of such documents is the instruction for the work of staff commands. In addition to that, in all rules, rules of battalions, brigades, companies, this process is detailed. This process entailed procedures and methods. Procedures were full and abbreviated. Those were the possible procedures. Or there was also a procedure without a consultation. What does this mean? Let us illustrate this through an example. A commander of a brigade with his command has a basic task, let's say. So he received a task from his superior, or perhaps he defined the task himself, this is irrelevant for our example. He studies the task. He gives guidance to the organs of command. He informs them of his design, if this is a so-called sector method. Mr. Theunens mentioned this in his report too. But if this is a team method, I can clarify if necessary, then the main design is not imparted to the rest; rather, the command proceeds immediately to assess the situation. If the sector method is applied, then the organs of command, upon receiving the task, upon hearing what the design of the brigade commander was, start preparing within their jurisdiction, proposals, proposals as to the resources they had under him. For example, they had assistant for intelligence affairs, or organ for intelligence affairs or, for example -- or assistants for operations affairs and so on, or they had, for example, assistants for atomic, biological, and chemical warfare, or for artillery, and other branches of service. So all of these staff organs of various specialties who are typically deployed to basic posts within the command post in accordance with a plan drafted by the assistant for operations affairs at the time specified by him submit their proposals. There are two ways, in principle, how these proposals can be adopted by the commander. The first method or the first way is as follows: As the organs submit their proposals, the commander can say, "I agree." I'm telling you this on the basis of my experience. Or the commander can say, "I disagree." The second way which is in compliance with the rules is to hear the proposal in full, the proposal of the command, and then the Chief of Staff who was simultaneously deputy commander proposes his own decision. The Chief of Staff in formulating his proposal does not need to repeat everything he heard from various specialty organs. He can say, for example, as the chief of artillery stated. Following that, commander takes the decision. He notifies the decision to the command organs. I said that in the staff there is the operations organ, who is in charge of converting the decision taken by the commander into an order that is sent down the chain of command. The difference between the commander's decision and the order or -- is in the first three items, because the commander's order contains, under number one, information about the enemy; under number two, the tasks conveyed to the brigades; item three, or point three, contains the information on neighbouring units. Now, from point four, or item four, until the end of the order, that is where the decision is contained. There is an office at the command, and the office staff will, together with the operations officer, draft the order. Now, this order, as a written document, is mandatory. It -- at the level of the command, it has to be drafted in writing and that is not an obligation for the lower levels. The brigade commander passes the order down to his subordinates, battalion commanders. This can be done in more than one way. One way is to -- for the commander to call them to his command post. The other way is that they call conduct command reconnaissance on the ground, which is most highly recommended of all the other ways but is extremely difficult in the conditions of a conflict taking place in built-up areas. The third way which is not recommended for such highly complex operations is that the order is submitted through communications officers in written form to subordinated commanders. This is the complete process all the way down to the battalion commander. When the battalion commander receives the order or the task, he acts upon it regardless of the way in which he received his task. The process will be the same, but not completely the same as in the brigade command because the battalion command doesn't have all the different specialty organs as the brigade command has. There's another difference here. To examine or review the task, this means to read the task that was produced in the written form and to fully comprehend it. Therefore, to read and understand what the intention of the brigade commander is, what his design and objective is, and what the task addressed to this particular battalion commander is, which assets are placed at his disposal, and when he is expected to be ready for combat. Now why is this important? According to the rules of service in the armed forces, the commander, or komandir, who did not fully understand the task assigned to him can contact his superior commander for additional clarifications. The commander who deems it impossible for him to implement the task can notify his superior commander as much -- accordingly, and it is for this reason that it is important for him to understand the task fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please, I want you to pause there and to know exactly what it is that you still wanted to say on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Your Honour, at this point, I believe this is a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. We must take the first break and we will resume at 25 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Unless I'm mistaken, in giving your answer, you came at the point of discussing this shortened procedure. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: The shortened procedure, unlike the full or complete procedure, is applied by those commands that do not have the time to apply the full procedure or the commands that are not fully staffed and therefore cannot carry out all these activities. At the level of the brigade command, the shortened procedure applied also means that the commander will develop the design and the order and then pass it down, either he or the Chief of Staff, whereupon a short assessment -- or a brief assessment of the situation is made or an assessment on such matters only as were selected by the commander. At the end of the process, the decision is taken and is passed down to the subordinate units. Thirdly -- or, rather, the third procedure under the rules is the "no consultation" procedure. The very name of the procedure clearly indicates that the commander is not bound to consult with anyone in the decision-making process. This particular procedure is not adequate for the brigade level. If such procedure is applied at the brigade level, however, then it is applied in the course of combat activities when rapid reaction is required to take a decision which deviates from the plan. Now we come to the battalion commander who will not have all the organs in his command as the brigade commander will. Therefore, it is appropriate for the battalion commander to apply the full procedure, shortened procedure, and no consultation procedure vis-a-vis his command organs as required by the situation. The company commander who does not have a command of his own or headquarters of his own will always have to apply the no consultation procedure because he doesn't have anyone to consult with. He himself assesses the situation, takes the decision and passes it down to his subordinates. His subordinates or the subordinates of the company commander are the platoon commander who is in a similar situation to that of the company commander and the squad commander who carries out the task. It is very important to note at this stage that the order as the initial document, a starting document, must be in writing at the brigade level. At the battalion level, the order is issued verbally and must not -- and need not necessarily be in written form. However, the most important parts of the order must be entered into the war diary. The war diary at the battalion level is kept by the deputy. It is not a document serving the purpose of command, but is kept as a record. The company platoon and squad commanders, therefore, this lowest level in the chain of command, will issue their orders verbally and need not produce a written document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Will you be so kind as to tell us now whether the Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica Detachment could be -- could have been resubordinated to the 1st Assault Detachment or the 3rd Motorised Company under the command of Miroslav Radic which was otherwise referred to, and we heard it in the courtroom, as --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Defence counsel please repeat the last word he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, could these two detachments have been resubordinated to the Assault Detachment 1 and whether they could have been resubordinated to the 3rd Motorised Company.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in answer to this question, I wish to state that my report was submitted in the month of August. As a member of the Defence team -- or, rather, members of the Defence team placed at my disposal voluminous material that they had in their possession. Presumably the same documents were in possession of the Prosecution. On the basis of the documents I had access to, and in response to this question, this is what I can state: The basic sources that can be of service are the order for blockade and attack by the commander of the Guards Brigade, and decisions to continue the attack on the town of Vukovar, as well as the handwritten diary or transcript of the diary done by the deputy commander of the 1st Battalion. The position of the instant detachments was, according to the documents I mentioned and to my understanding of them, as follows: The Petrova Gora detachment, in initial combat operations, that's to say in the order to lay down the blockade and launch an attack, that's Exhibit 405, issued by the commander of the Guards Brigade was not part of the composition of the Guards Brigade. That this is, in fact, true is indicated by item 2 of the order. It was established at item 2 of the order lays down the tasks of the instant unit, in this case, the Guards Brigade. I have to say that I did not have insight into the document whereby the Guards Brigade received the task in -- concerning the attack on Vukovar. I have the document entitled "order for blockade and attack" from the commander of the Guards Brigade, and we stated that -- said that under item 2, the task of the brigade was set out. There, it reads that the Petrova Gora detachment is the neighbour of the Guards Brigade, which means that it was not within or subordinated to the commander of the Guards Brigade. The next decision involving the continuation of the attack on Vukovar dated 15 October.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes, 1991. Exhibit 408.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Exhibit number 408. Mr. Forca, pause there. If my learned friends deem it necessary, we can place the document on the ELMO, but I do believe you have the documents and we can proceed this way. Thank you. Carry on, Professor.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: This exhibit shows that the said Petrova Gora detachment was part of Operations Group South and that it acted in coordination with the Assault Detachment 1. Specifically in the tasks assigned to units under point 2 concerning JOD 1, its composition is stated, and it reads: "In coordination with JOD 2, 3/211 Armoured Brigade," which means the 3rd Battalion of the armoured brigade, "and with the units of Petrova Gora." Therefore, JOD 1 and the Petrova Gora detachment act in coordination. In the following document, decision to continue the attack on Vukovar -- or, rather, to continue the Vukovar operation, Exhibit 410, the Leva Supoderica detachment is mentioned for the first time, as far as I was able to see. It is quite evident from the tasks assigned to the units that they were subordinated to JOD 1, because the document reads: "JOD comprises 1st Motorised Battalion, one platoon of the 3rd Company of the 2nd Military Police Battalion, Leva Supoderica detachment, Petrova Gora detachment." Therefore, these are the units within that formation as well as other ones, the composition of the 1st JOD. And there the detachments subordinated to the commanders are also listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Which date is that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: 29th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please, sir, try to slow down a little and I'll do my best too.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: I understand. The document dated 0800 hours on the 14th of November, 1991, produced by Operations Group South command 398-1, Exhibit 430, the commander decides and issues the following orders in item 4, specifically: The following unit is detached from JOD 1, the 1st Motorised Battalion. And a special task is given to JOD 1, while in item 5 or, rather, item 2, tasks for units under 5, a special task is given to the 1st Motorised Battalion. Now, the answer. Who were they subordinated to? The Petrova Gora detachment and the Leva Supoderica detachment. In practical terms, there can be two answers. It is possible that they remained subordinated to the command of JOD 1 which, as of the 1st of October, 1991, was the -- a post occupied by the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion because that is what the first order by the brigade commander says. Alternatively, it could be to the commander of OG South. Because the task was given to the detachment by the commander of OG South. And the last in this series of documents is the decision and order by the commander of OG South dated 1900 hours on the 16th of November, 1991, 431.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Exhibit 431?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Exhibit 431. Where there is an addendum -- or, rather, a new task is issued to the 1st Battalion under item 1 -- item 2, actually, paragraph 2, item 1. The 1st Motorised Battalion, in keeping with the task issued on the 14th, which means two days previously in relation to that previous one, and now, there is the task given to the 1st Motorised Battalion. In item 2, tasks, but under 10, as there is no explicit reference to JOD 1, it can be understood that its task was the same as that issued on the 14th of November because that's what item 10 says. "The remaining units of OG South will be used in keeping with the previous decision," and then in brackets, the 14th of November. It is along these lines that the Petrova Gora detachment and at a later stage, the Leva Supoderica detachment, based on the documents I have referred to, based on the documents available, could have been under the command initially of OG South but not the Guards Brigade. In later operations, they could again have been under the command of OG South but now also the commander of the Guards Brigade who is also the commander of OG South; whereas during the final operations, they could have been under the command of the commander of OG South or the commander of the 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Forca, would you be so kind as to explain the term "until the completion of the mission." You talked about temporary formations, and you used this phrase "until the completion of the task or mission." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you allow -- I am a scientist. If you allow, I will approach this phrase, "the completion of a task," from a practical position. This phrase, "the completion of a task," involves two concepts; the first being the concept of task, and the other being the concept of completion. Each of these two concepts, plus the overriding concept of the completion of a task, have their own definitions. In the literature, that means if you go to the military lexicon, to the military encyclopedia, a task is related to an objective that must be reached by using certain forces in a certain area over a certain time period. In addition to that principal meaning of the concept of task, a task is also an element in an order, and as we have already said, one of these elements is normally tasks for units. "To complete" is a verb which means to complete an activity, to get something done. Therefore, the phrase "until the completion of the task," means that those forces specified in an order, in an area that they were designated and assigned must carry out such objectives as have been assigned to them over a specified period of time. From the brigade level, or rather the level of OG South down to the lowest possible level of control -- command and control, which is the squad level, and especially the temporary formations, there are large-scale differences involved. To complete a task, what does that mean for a brigade? We must go back to the order given by the brigade commander. What does it mean to complete a task contained in a decision? To complete a task in terms of JOD 1 or the 1st Motorised Battalion requires a lot less space, a lot less time, and a lot less manpower. But if we look up the assault detachment level, there can be a great many small individual tasks which unfortunately we can hardly now be expected to specify since we do not have a written document to this effect. However, we are able to assume, based on how the operations unfolded each task that had specified areas, time period, or manpower, was carried out. If the assault group within JOD 1, for example, had the task of taking a certain house or a certain street, having done this, the assault group thereby completed its task. Sure enough, some tasks don't necessarily coincide with the general task that, for example, Operations Group South had. What is particularly important during the completion of a task, if you have this phrase, "the completion of a task," is the information dimension. Now what exactly is this a reference to? Please allow me to quote an example by Tofflers in their book, "War and Anti-War." This is what they said back in 1815 in the New Orleans battle, 2.000 British and American soldiers killed each other because the news of a cease-fire signed in Geneva was seven days late. If the news had arrived in time, 2.000 people would have remained alive. Things being what they were, they killed each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Professor Forca, let us leave this issue aside for the time being. At the time, in 1991, do you know if party affiliations or political organisation were allowed in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Of course I do know that, since I was a member of the JNA at the time. What I wish to say now is not only was it not allowed, it was strictly forbidden in the JNA. I provided a reference to a document, a collection of documents from the defence and safety of Yugoslavia in 1990 and 1991. This was published by the military publishing house, VIZ in Belgrade in 2000. There is reference there to a document banning any form of party activity in the JNA. This is an order of the federal secretary for All People's Defence dated the 8th of October, 1991. Item 1 of this order says: "Any form of political or party activity in command staffs, units, or military institutions shall be strictly forbidden." This order is in reference to the TO as well, because as is well known, the armed forces comprised both the JNA and the TO. Item 5 of the specified order, which had a total of five items, so the last one contains the following order: "All of the army must be familiarised with this order."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would you please be so kind as to say -- take the Vukovar operation as an example, what is the difference between organisation informational [as interpreted] structure and the combat disposition? In this operation, for example.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, for those who have my report, take a -- have a look, this is at page 70 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please specify the paragraph number?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: It's 58. 58 in part 2 of my report, as well as the following page, page 71, paragraph 60. In one of my previous answers, I explain the difference between what is establishment and what is temporary. Each JNA unit had an organisational structure and formation that were -- or establishment that were precisely defined. It's called the organisational and establishment structure. Speaking of organisation, organisation of a unit, what this normally means is that this unit had a command, a commanding element, if you like, a combat element, a security element, and a support element. Speaking of establishment, what that means is that the manpower and the equipment are precisely specified. One must know in relation to this that companies are the basic tactical units and a battalion is a basic joint tactical unit, and these were forms of establishment that could not be altered or changed. Each infantry company had a precisely pre-determined or specified number of men and pieces of equipment. An organisational structure which has a command, the 1st Motorised Battalion, the 2rd Motorised Battalion, the 1st Armoured and the rest, the Howitzer battalion and all the other units, in order to complete a task, this is transformed by a decision into a functional structure, and you can see that at page 71, paragraph 60. The diagram from paragraph 58 is a chart, an organisation chart for OG South made up of the units specified in the chart. The Guards Brigade plus reinforcements by the decision of the commander of OG South by the 15th day of October, because that is the example that I chose, since that was an excellent example of an order well written and a well-written decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you can have this displayed in the e-court system. It's even done in colour there which makes for ease of handling.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, please continue.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: The organisation of OG South is converted into elements of combat disposition or order. These elements are no longer called 1st Motorised Battalion, 2nd Motorised Battalion, but are now elements of combat disposition. As you can see in paragraph 60, on the left-hand side, the colour should be yellow, designating the forces -- the assault forces. You can see that in terms of establishment, these are units with reinforcements making up the assault utilities; that's JOD 1, JOD 2, JOD 3, JOD 4, 20th Partisan Brigade, 3rd Battalion of the 211th Armoured Brigade, and TO detachment Petrova Gora. So you see that a unit which has an establishment also becomes an element within the combat disposition, but not only do they have the command organs, they also have communications units. On the right-hand side in red colour are marked the other elements of the combat disposition involved. You can see that there are three artillery battalions but only one of the elements is the fire support unit. You have the anti-aircraft defence units -- or, rather, the PVO artillery battalion, you have the territorial units which were assigned to Sremska Mitrovica detachment by that commander, and security forces consisting of the units mentioned herein. The logistics battalion, the ABHO platoon, and so on. In this order, there was the armoured battalion of the brigade that was the main organisational element, so there is a large difference between the organisational and establishment structure and combat disposition. The organisational and establishment structure of each and every unit is defined in very specific terms. The strength of the units making up a certain combat disposition is not defined by their establishment but pursuant to a decision taken in a very specific situation, and that is the essential difference between the two different elements and structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe you've clarified this. Can you tell us: In your view until what time was there a need for assault detachments and groups to exist?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: We talked about what it means to complete a task. As the commander ordered in his order dated -- he says, "I decided in the course of the night before dawn on -- that on the 2nd of October lines should be deployed to the contact line and then with air and artillery support, wherein the artillery support should last for 20 minutes, engage fiercefully in an attack in the area assigned in coordination with JTO," which means TO units, "and JNA units with the following objective: To crush enemy forces, take control of the town, and to cease all the activities within the area of the Guards Brigade." The rest of the order is not relevant for my answer. On the 18th of November, 1991, according to the documents available, the last group surrendered at Mitnica whereby, de facto, the need for the existence of assault detachments no longer existed or ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: This also applies to assault groups as well, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps for the assault groups the need ceased even earlier because they are lower-level units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Forca, what is the observation post of the commander of a company in a situation where there is an attack on an inhabited area, and I mean in the course of the attack itself?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: We have already discussed the terms "observation post" and "command post" and the difference between the two. This question refers to the observation post in the event of an attack on a built-up area. You see, all the rules of engagement treat the attack as one form of combat action. In this context, when we are talking about the company commander's observation post, this is regulated by the rules of companies. Since this is a very specific form of combat, in addition to the general provisions governing attack or assault as one form of combat, or rather, one aspect of combat, not one form of combat as the Prosecution expert report stated, there are specific provisions governing assault in a woodland area or on a river-crossing and specifically an attack on a built-up area. In this context, the observation post of a company commander in the course of an attack on a built-up area will not be the same as the observation post of a company commander involved in a classical attack on a hilly area. The observation post of the company commander who, under the rules, must always issue orders directly on the ground, will always be wherever the company commander is. This need not necessarily be a fixed observation post that must be on that same location over a longer period as would be the case in a classical attack. In an attack on a built-up area, the company commander issues order on the ground, and the observation post of the company commander is the location at which he is to be found at a given time. Depending on the attack, it can be 1, 5, 10, or even 50 different houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Forca, in the event of an attack on a built-up area, the company commander or the company itself uses communications means in a built-up area. Which means of communication are used in an attack on a built-up area?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honour, an explicit answer to this question can be found in the rules governing companies and platoons. The main means of communications used in an attack on a built-up area is radio communications. There are many reasons behind that and they are quite evident when one knows all the means of communication available. Historically speaking, and in terms of military experience, one of the most frequent attacks is the attack on a built-up area. From that point of departure, and keeping in mind the means available to the commander, the communication by couriers is to be strictly avoided because radio communication and all the devices necessary for it available to the commander will not entail manpower as is necessary in the case when a courier is applied who needs to pass a certain distance. That is why radio communication is preferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When speaking of radio communication, is the network of Motorolas that sort of communication?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes, a Motorola is radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned couriers. Under the rules and based on experience in practice, who and how designates couriers for company commanders?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: In the rules on -- of communications, there is one provision stipulating that the communication will be chosen by the superior and the subordinate will be held accountable for it, which means that in the case of couriers, the company commander has three platoons, if we're speaking of the specific commander of the 3rd Company. Every platoon is duty-bound to designate a courier for the company commander because the company commander himself doesn't have couriers. The same will be done by the company commander if the battalion commander requests that courier service be established between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In view of some evidence we've heard before this Tribunal, I have the following question to you which is very important for the Tribunal: What is the relationship between the brigade security organs and company commanders in combat? And of course I'm referring to specific combat situations.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Generally speaking about security - thank you - we normally touch upon two aspects; the general security aspect and the counter-intelligence aspect. The security organ -- I have to apologise because I have not been a security organ and have never dealt with these matters but I know the rules, and under the rules, the security organ will carry out these other activities, notably counter-intelligence activities. In performing these duties, the security organ may also be involved in the detection of crime and causes and other elements that have a bearing on the security situation. The general security aspect lies within the competence of command and not counter-intelligence, that is to say the command does not deal with counter-intelligence but with the general security situation, the protection of plan manpower, equipment, data protection and so on. In this sense, the security organ of the command and the security organ can and must cooperate. The company commander who is tasked with general security need not know, nor is the security organ duty-bound to inform him thereof what the reasons and methods applied by the security organ are.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, can you tell us what the notion of the town command is, how it is set up and by whom, and can you tell us what are the duties of the town commander under the rules?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: If you will allow me a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: In the documents of Operations Group South and orders and related documents issued by the commander of the 1st Military District, on several occasions it was ordered that town commands be set up. By way of an example, I can refer you to the order from the commander of Operations Group South dated 9 November 1991. The order bears the following number, 340-1, wherein it is stated that: "Commands are set up in the villages of Negoslavci comprising the following," and now Ljubisa Vukasinovic is mentioned as town commander, Deputy Captain Bozic, and Janko Sretko [as interpreted] is there as the subordinate. And then Jabukovac, Grabovo, and the village of Berak mentioned as locations where town commands are set up. In these -- or, rather, in this document orders were issued designating certain persons, and it reads there that the authority is set up in accordance with the rules of service and that all measures are to be taken with a view to preventing incursions by sabotage, terrorist groups and preventing terrorist actions. It is also ordered that instructions be set up governing their work and that conditions be created for life and work of the population. I have to actually start from the latter and state that as an expert witness, I did not have occasion to see the instruction governing the work of the town command, and I can only assume that the town commands worked as per rules. Specifically, in the town of Vukovar, persons were appointed town commanders who came from the level of battalions or artillery battalions and, as we were able to see from this specific example, from the command. Mr. Vukasinovic came from the command of the Guards Brigade, specifically from the security organ; he was deputy chief of security. Therefore, company commanders could not have been, nor were they appointed town commanders. The commander of the Guards Brigade issued the orders that we mentioned on how town commands were to be organised. By the same token, his subordinate commander, specifically the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, in keeping with the order issued by the commander of the Guards Brigade or OG South, issued their own orders to set up town commands -- or, rather, command posts. As we said, town commands must be set up in keeping with the rules of service. The rules of service make no reference to town commands; rather, there are references to garrisons. That is in item 78. And then it goes on to explain what a garrison is, who is appointed garrison commander, the sort of business to be conducted in a garrison, and so on and so forth. This is then associated with the order saying that one must act in keeping with the rules of service and along the following principle: Garrison, garrison command, and then back to the order that was issued. What is obvious is this: In terms of discipline, the town commander was the superior of whoever happened to be there. This means he was not required to give them any assignments in the sense of combat operations or even try to affect their -- whatever assignments they happen to have. What he was required to do, however, was to make sure there was order and to make sure there was discipline. And that's what the order says, even to prevent mistreatment. In terms of practical experience, it is generally known that a town commander, as the order says he must prevent any incursions by sabotage and other groups, was required to determine call-signs which means that the place occupied by the commander could not possibly have been accessed by anyone without this person's presence becoming known.
