The principal reason for this is the order that came from the brigade commander, the commander of OG South, but it was also to protect his own men and ensure there was discipline in his area of responsibility, because all persons moving about that area, going from one place to another, had to know this. He had to make sure they knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. Regardless of the town commander, let me ask you something that we want to know here in this courtroom. Who has the power to order the commander of a brigade's military police unit anything, who has the power to issue him orders?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Specifically in the Vukovar operation we had two different levels of military police units. These were the military police battalions, the 1st and the 2nd, and the Guards Brigade, and the military police company in the 80th Motorised Brigade. As there was a linear command system in place, the tasks to all commanders in the brigade, and I mean the Guards Brigade, the battalion, or the directly subordinate ones, when talking about the 80th Motorised Brigade, all these tasks are issued by the brigade commander. Or, rather, this can also be done by his deputy in the commander's absence with the commander's approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But there were those brigades who also had a military police company; for example, the 80th Motorised Brigade. Can you please tell us who was in charge of issuing orders to the commander of the military police there? There is a specific example from Vukovar that we have.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes, in the 80th Motorised Brigade, the person who had the power to issue assignments to the military police commander was the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. It says the komandir of the military police company and the transcript says commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, in a company say commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. The commander of the military police company of the 80th Motorised Brigade. Who would have had the power to issue them any orders?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: According to the rules, it would have been his superior. In terms of the linear system of command, his superior would have been the commander of the 80th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the Chief of Staff? Would he also have had the power to issue him orders to him?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes, having previously been authorised by his own commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Another question about this, if you don't mind: What about the commander of an infantry company? Can he be in command of a military police company? For example, the commander of the 3rd Motorised Company, could he have been in command of another military police company or not?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: A company commander doesn't have the required level of training, nor can he do this in terms of the establishment. So the answer to your question is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During an attack, who is appointed to what is normally referred to as the main axis of attack, both in theory and in practice?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Both in terms of the rules and in terms of practical experience it is the best trained units that are sent there. When I say "the best trained units," what I mean is these are the best trained men from that unit. They have the best possible equipment available to their unit and, in particular, the units morale has to be exceptionally high.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Forca, you provided some conclusions that you attached to the -- your expert report. We want to know about some specific conclusions. Can you please go to number 24 and can you read it out for our benefit, please? This is item 24 of your conclusion. Before you do that or rather -- go ahead, please. We can't go through all the conclusions, we simply don't have the time, and I want to focus on this one now.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: "Commander of the 3rd Motorised Company of the 1st Motorised Battalion, according to the 1st MTB command documents, commander of the 3rd Motorised Company of the 1st Motorised Brigade, Captain Miroslav Radic, in combat operations, carried out the functional duty, commander of the 3rd Assault Group. In the initial operations, TO Vukovar units Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica detachments engaged in coordinated actions with it. Tasks issued by the commander" --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: "Tasks issued by the commander of the 1st JOD were received at the same time by Captain Radic and the commander of TO Vukovar Dusan Jaksic, later Miroljub Vujevic, as well as the commander of the Leva Supoderica Detachment, Milan Lancuzanin, Kameni, from the time these detachments were attached to JOD 1," or the 1st Motorised Battalion. In other words, Captain Miroslav Radic was not the superior of the commanders of the above-mentioned TO detachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You will probably have occasion to interpret all these other conclusions when cross-examined by the OTP. Just to make sure there is no doubt about this, can you please explain what item 27 means, where you mention a certain TO? The question is: Which specific TO units that you have in mind and what exactly does this mean? Before I go on with the other items.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Shall I read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, silently, please, just tell us what it means. You can read it out for the benefit of the Chamber, actually.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: "The engagement of the 3rd Motorised Company as the 3rd Assault Group in combat operations in Operation Vukovar lasted until the seizure of Milovo Brdo, 10th of November, 1991, according to the diary of the 1st Motorised Battalion and the latest until the 14th of November, 1991. More precisely, until the decision of the OG South commander, strictly confidential number 398-1, at 0800 hours, on the 14th of November, 1991. As of that time, all TO units were excluded from the complement of the 3rd Assault Group and were not under the command of Captain Miroslav Radic."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is precisely this last sentence. Can you please explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I have pointed out already, while writing my report, the report that was submitted to you, I used, above all, numerous documents among which I referred in my previous testimony the decisions by the OG South commander as well as handwritten copies of the war log of the 1st Motorised Battalion which was produced by the deputy commander. What this means is that this order means the following: When Milovo Brdo was taken on the 10th of November, 1991, any reasons for the existence of the 3rd Assault Group ceased to exist. This group was mentioned in the handwritten copy of the log written by the deputy commander of the 1st Battalion. He referred to the 3rd Company in this document as the 3rd Assault Group. By the decision of the commander of OG South dated the 14th of November, the 1st Motorised Battalion and JOD 1 were physically separated. And also in terms of their assignment, the 1st Motorised Battalion, which is an establishment unit, now received a different assignment. During the fighting, units of the 1st Motorised Battalion were joined by members of the TO and volunteers, most of them from the Republic of Serbia. That is the meaning of this last sentence. All those who were assigned to the 3rd Company, which the deputy commander described as an assault group, were pulled out from the company, and as of the 10th, to all practical purposes, at least based on the log that was written, or pursuant to the 14th of November decision, all Captain Radic was left with were the recruits, conscripts doing their military term.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain this, too, and try to be as precise as possible: When we say TO units, TO units that were pulled out, does that mean the Petrova Gora detachment and the Leva Supoderica detachment or not, does that include those two detachments?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: No, it doesn't

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You're positive, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind - we're nearing the end of the examination-in-chief - as to read out item number 29, your conclusion number 29.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: "Captain Miroslav Radic's unit - the 3rd Motorised Company, a mere establishment formation after the seizure of Milovo Brdo - carried out the regular tasks after the conclusion of combat operations and was preparing for its return to Belgrade, making sure to take all appropriate security measures in their own deployment sector until their return on the 24th of November, 1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we break for lunch, will you please make an effort and tell the Trial Chamber what conclusion number 30 of your report says and then we'll no longer be reading these. I suppose you still abide by everything that you wrote there, right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes. Number 30: "Establishment units, commanded by Captain Miroslav Radic, upon the seizure of Vukovar, no earlier than the 18th of November, 1991, did not have any tasks related to the transport or security of the convoy of captured Croatian paramilitary formations, civilians and wounded. It can be asserted with certainty that the 3rd Motorised Company, Captain Radic, only the soldiers received a verbal order via the communications system and a task from the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion to provide security for the hospital grounds in Vukovar on the 19th of November, 1991. "In the late afternoon hours on the 19th of November, 1991, the units of the 3rd Motorised Company securing the hospital in Vukovar were relieved by a military police unit (the 2nd Battalion of the military police) which is in fact a military police task."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUDURIC
utterances.text: And finally, "FRY government report to the commission of expert established pursuant to security council resolution, number 780/92, Belgrade, dated 3rd November, 1992," e-court reference 2D12-1317.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 812, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to thank the better part of my team.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, is there anything you would like to say concerning your expert report, as I have finished my examination-in-chief? Is there anything you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Borovic, I can only repeat what I have already said and that is that the report was submitted in August due to translation and other procedures. It was drafted in this form on the basis of the documents the Defence sent to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I said, I have completed my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Professor.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My name is Vladimir Domazet. I am one of the lawyers for Mr. Mrksic, and on behalf of his Defence I will put several questions to you. First, I would like to discuss the first part of your expert [as interpreted]. Wherever possible, I will refer to page numbers and paragraph numbers for the benefit for the two of us and for the benefit of the parties to the proceedings. Let us also be mindful of the fact that we have to speak slowly in order for the transcript to accurately reflect whatever we say. On page 11 of your report, you speak of the Guards Motorised Brigade as an elite unit in terms of human and material resources, but particularly in reference to human resources. I will have no questions on this matter because you have been quite clear in your report. I would put a different question to you as a military expert: Did you take into account certain decisions of the 1st Military District -- or, rather, you did take them into account concerning the operation of Vukovar. Do you think, as an expert, that it was warranted for such a unit which had specific purposes to be used for Operation Vukovar, for the purposes it was used?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honour, all the units of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army had specifically defined tasks and competencies, the task of priority of the Guards Motorised Brigade was not the task it was in fact used for. My expertise dealt with control from the squad to the brigade level primarily. This is what I can say in response to Mr. Domazet's question. First, I, as an expert, don't know why the Guards Brigade was used for Operation Vukovar. I can assume, and I repeat I can only assume, that knowing what the composition of the Guards Brigade was and the high quality it exhibited, and knowing the level of responsibility of the military personnel, be it officers or ordinary soldiers, the military leadership relied on these factors in issuing the -- such an order to the Guards Motorised Brigade which was not primarily intended for that particular task. I say this without knowing what the reasons behind the order and the decision were. I know that the units are best employed and used for the purposes they were initially intended. I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I have two questions concerning what you stated on page 47 on the issue of command responsibility and the responsibility of superiors. That's in paragraphs 113 and 119. You mentioned the instructions on the application of the international laws of war in the armed forces of SFRY from 1988. First of all, I'd like to know whether this also applied in the event of an aggression on the SFRY and the international conflict or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He's asking for a legal opinion as to the application of certain international rules to -- what he describes as "an aggression."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are here asking about matters of law, are you not, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is true, Your Honour, that I am putting this question if the expert witness, who is a professor and a doctor of military science knows the answer to this. In paragraph 119, he also spoke of another matter that I wanted to deal with, another point of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The problem with points of law, Mr. Domazet, is that it is the role of this Chamber to decide questions of law and the subject matter isn't even one of particular expertise about the law in the former Yugoslavia. And further, while the witness may be eminent in his knowledge of certain aspects of the military, it does not appear that he would claim to be an expert military lawyer. So I think that your question really has to be put aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will not be asking the question then. The interpretation of it by the witness in item 119 is of a rather legal nature, but then I suppose I won't be asking any questions about that either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Forca, can you please look at paragraph 55, this is page 68. Your comment in this paragraph, do I understand it correctly as your criticism of the way the command of the 1st Military District organised Operations Group South. You seem to be saying that this was done in a fashion that was contrary to the theory, and the rules for the reason you explained here: "Operations Group is superior to a brigade and a special command must be assigned." Can you please elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, as Mr. Domazet has just stated, in paragraph 55, I criticise the way Operations Group South was set up. When I say the way Operations Group South was set up, I mean from the moment when the responsibility of the commander of OG South was taken over by Colonel Mrksic. Having studied the theory behind temporary formations, the theory specified in my reports where it addresses temporary formations, and I can also say that OTP expert witnesses seem to have referred to more or less the same or similar documents, I have come across several definitions provided by experts. Above all, in the document that has now been officially admitted, some questions and issues concerning command and control in the armed forces of the SFRY, again temporary formations are considered, and in these theoretical sources, where there is reference to an operations unit or a temporary group, a definition is always provided as to what it is made up of. It can be made up of a corps, a division, or several brigades. This is a level which is not prescribed, at least not the way it is organised such as the case may be with a brigade, a division, or a corps. Among other things, when you set up an operations group by setting up several brigades, in principle, the recommended course of action is to set up a special command which, in the specific case of Operations Group South, was simply not done. Operations Group South comprised the Guards Brigade, the 20th Partisan Brigade, and the 80th Motorised Brigade, at least throughout the period of time that I analysed in my report. What actually happened was units of the same level being resubordinated to the commander of the Guards Brigade who then became the commander of the operations group. Brigade level units were subordinated to him, resubordinated to him. I analysed this in the latter part of my report, what the effects of these actions were. Just to give you an example, the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade was at the same level as his company commander. There is an order by Commander Mrksic or a decision that we mentioned saying that the reconnaissance company of that brigade was the reserve force as an element of its combat disposition. Now, as the commander who is in command of any element of the combat position. Secondly, given the way that the composition of the operations group was determined, brigade commanders and battalion commanders were brought up to the same level because the commander of Assault Detachment 1 or the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion was first subordinated to the commander of the Guards Brigade or the commander of OG South. Along these lines, and bearing in mind everything that I have just told you as well as my research on the subject, I believe that the command of the 1st Military District did not act in keeping with these provisions when they set up the operations group, especially as of the moment when Colonel Mrksic took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you think this affected the exercising of command in any way?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: To be quite honest, the execution of a task is closely linked to the rules of service. A task which is received must be carried out. Given the particular features of the officers involved in the Guards Brigade and their men, I suppose they accepted this task and of course that sort of thing does have a bearing on how command is exercised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please go to paragraph 45 on page 66 of the B/C/S. Here you address the operations area of the Guards Motorised Brigade and OG South at an early stage in operations. Further down you provide the exact boundaries of that area, and you say that the Vukovar Hospital lay outside the operations area covered by OG South until the 19th of November, 1991, when the order came that you quote. Is my understanding correct, sir? The reason I'm asking this is there was an OTP witness, it was Trifunovic, I think, who said that the hospital did in fact lie within the operations area of OG South?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on the documents that were available to me -- or, rather, each area has four dimensions: The front, the rear, the left, and the right. As for what Mr. Domazet's question is about is the front. According to documents where commanders address the issue of the area, the Guards Brigade with OG South was attacking as far as the River Vuka. As for as the area across the River Vuka, the unit attacking there was Tactical Group North. It was for this reason that I understood the commander of the 1st Military District to have issued an order for the Guards Brigade or, rather, for OG South to continue the operation and take the hospital. I interpreted this to effectively mean an extension of the area covered by the Guards Brigade or OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. One of the last sentences there, the task to go towards the hospital in coordination with TG North. Does that mean that TG North continued to be responsible for that or does it not mean that at all?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Can you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Look at the last answer.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes, I've gone through it, but what exactly do you want me to answer. Where is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It says: "Because it was OG South, they brought the task in coordination to TG North to take the hospital on the 19th November by 1000 hours."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: In keeping with what I was saying about coordination, the task given to TG North implied more or less the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we now please go to paragraph 101 on page 86 of the B/C/S version of the report. You address the evacuation of the hospital, and you say that this was an activity of the greatest possible importance with security organs of the Federal Secretariat for All People's Defence being involved, and you go on to quote a portion of the war log. In your opinion, what would the arrival of a team like that mean, a security organ of the Federal Secretariat for the All People's Defence, specifically their arrival there for the evacuation of the hospital or any of the related missions?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know exactly what it meant, meaning I don't have any document ordering those bodies to go to the area of OG South. However, if we look at some other documents, it can be deduced that these organs were supposed to conduct a triage of those present at the hospital, since there was every indication at the time that not everybody taking shelter at the hospital was the sick and wounded by rather those who weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, based on what you just told us, one of their tasks was to get involved in the selection and separation of those members from the civilians -- the civilians at the hospital specifically. That's what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes, separating the wounded and injured -- separating them from the wounded and injured who belonged in the hospital anyway, by rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You will remember that you referred to the presence of Colonel Nebojsa Pavkovic, the then Colonel Nebojsa Pavkovic, you remember that? And according to your research, was Colonel Nebojsa Pavkovic there and in just what capacity?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: As for the presence of General Pavkovic, there's an order to that effect issued by the chef du cabinet of the Federal Secretariat for All People's Defence mentioning that he would be there on their behalf in the Vukovar operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the presence of such a high-ranking officer from the cabinet of the federal secretary for All People's Defence? Would that not indicate that the Federal Secretariat deemed the Vukovar operation and what was going on there at the time as a matter of particular significance?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: I think -- yes, I think that's exactly what it might be taken to mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you now please go to paragraph 115 at page 92 of the B/C/S. It seems that based on the documents available to you, there are three things that remain insufficiently clarified which you state under A, B, and C respectively. What I want to know about is the one under B. You believe one thing that remains unclear is just who ordered the military police unit of the 80th Motorised Brigade to guard prisoners at Ovcara on the 20th of November. My question is: According to the regulations, who would have had the power to issue an order like that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I have said already, the question was raised about the regulations and who would have had the power to issue orders to the commander of the military police or the battalion commander. It could have been the brigade commander, he would have had the power to issue orders to the commander of the MP company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That means the commander of the 80th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes, that is indeed what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you have look to see what was recorded in the operations log of the 80th Brigade in relation to the 20th and securing the prisoners and securing Ovcara, since there is a reference to that in the log?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes. What I used in my report is the fact -- rather, that can be found in the documents; namely, that the security detail withdrew at around 2200 hours, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But that's not the entry that I meant. I meant the entry that the prisoners would come. It doesn't reflect who ordered it but I had in mind the previous entry that the arrival is expected. Only if you remember that, otherwise not, because we have the other information that you mentioned in our evidence. Mr. Forca, I would now like to go back to the second part where you analyse the Vukovar operation and the then situation both in the JNA and in the Territorial Defence. You were quite detailed there. I will skip all of those parts that are not relevant in my view. First of all, a little bit about the National Guards Corps. You, as a military expert, what can you tell us about the ZNG and what it represented at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, in reply to this question, I wish to say the following: The second part of the Operation Vukovar, and its first subpart and the activities - this is something that you can see in one of the conclusions - it is necessary to analyse the conditions, the circumstances under which "one little company commander" found himself. I apologise to the commander of the 3rd Company for calling him a little, insignificant commander. All I wanted was to describe and to make it clear to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question is: Could you please -- or basically I'm summarising it, tell us about the National Guards Corps or the ZNG, and the witness is now talking about the circumstances in which one little company commander found himself. And he's talking about Mr. Radic and the situation where he found himself. That's not the question. The question is: Please tell us about the National Guards Corps. He's off on another tangent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not really a point of objection, Mr. Weiner. But you will understand that you were asked about a topic that was different and you've gone to something else. If you would be able to come back to the ZNG, that is what Mr. Domazet would like your assistance with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Forca. The question was about the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Your Honours, I apologise for making such a long introduction, but I wanted to say that -- and this is reflected in the footnote, the bit about ZNG, I wanted to say that I took this over from Professor Radovan Radinovic from the general part in the Kunarac case. However, as I can see, this was not admitted into evidence, and my reply to Mr. Domazet is that these views were taken over from Professor Radinovic who was a military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, when speaking of what occurred in the first half of 1991 in Croatia, paragraphs 6 and 7 on page 52, you also speak of the beginning of some spontaneous resistance in the areas of Croatia where Serbs constituted a majority. And then in paragraph 7, you speak of two processes. The first one was the paramilitary organisation and arming of Croatia and its multiple preparation for war, and the second one is organisation of the Serbian people in Croatia for self-defence. My question is whether these two facts are interlinked and can you give us a bit of a broader explanation? Can you expand on this?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, yet again I have to say to Mr. Domazet that these views were taken over from Professor Radinovic, from his expert analysis. They were included here in order to illustrate the background, to illustrate what preceded the Vukovar operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, you explained that. But given that you referred to it, does this mean that you accept these views and that you included them in your report, regardless of where they come from, but you included them in your report as part of your own opinion?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: This is the opinion of Professor Radinovic and I as an expert consider it to be acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Would you please look at paragraph 12 on the following day where you quote a speech of the Croatian president Franjo Tudjman. Would you please read the words that follow "on the Ban Jelacic Square"? Read the text in quotation marks which is what Tudjman stated at the time on the 24th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Under quotation marks: "There would have been no war if Croatia had not wanted it, but we assess that the only way to win Croatia's independence was through war. This is why we held political negotiations and while these negotiations were in progress, we formed our own armed units. If we had not done so, we would not have reached our goal. So war could have been avoided only if we had given up our goals, that is to say, the independence of our state."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now that we are dealing with this, there was a question put to you by Mr. Borovic where you explained the role of the JNA in the fall of 1991; you gave us several elements. What I am interested in is your assessment, based on everything you have done so far, about the role of the JNA in the first half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we just specify whether the first half means including June?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I didn't focus on this. This wasn't the focus of my research, the role of the JNA during that period of time. However, what can be considered as something that is generally known during that period of time, there were already conflicts within the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, namely in Slovenia, and in Borovo -- or, rather, in some settlements, some towns in Croatia. If I had to give you my opinion about the role of the JNA - how should I put it? - not in the sense of what was ordered to the JNA but in the sense of how I, as an expert, see the role of the JNA during that period of time, then I would say that the role could be defined as separating two belligerent sides or two sides to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Something concerning paragraph 14 and what you described in detail there. This concerns the incident in Borovo Selo which took place in May, on the 2nd of May, 1991. I believe this to be quite important because this event was mentioned by a lot of OTP witnesses as an event which was a turning point in the events in Vukovar. The Serbs stopped going to work after that, barricades were erected and so on. Thus, I think that it is extremely important to establish what actually took place on that day in Borovo Selo. You described this in detail here, and I do not wish to repeat this, but tell us this: You say that there were five buses with armed policemen. So based on that, can you tell us how many policemen intervened and how can that be related to the number of casualties, both those who were killed and wounded after the conflict? So would you tell us whether, in your experience, such an operation would be justified or not? And the role of the JNA is also mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honour, as is stated here, the Presidency established that the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, through a consistent and resolute engagement in the implementation of its constitutional duties again managed in extremely difficult circumstances to reduce and stop the spreading of interethnic conflicts. This means that the statement which can be found in the collection of documents which were admitted into evidence today as Exhibit - just a minute please - 806, that during that period of time, which is to say the first half of 1991, the JNA was involved in separating two warring parties. Naturally, all of those who, during that time, were in the area and who received various information can possibly have a different opinion from their own point of view. In reply to your question, all I can say is that in that sense, the JNA separated the warring sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question on this topic. Would you please look at paragraph 39, which is page 62 in your copy. In reply to a question put to you by Mr. Borovic, you touched upon this subject, thus there is no need to repeat. All I am interested in is this: You speak about the Vukovar operation, and I would like to know whether this is your personal criticism of the decision of the commander of the 1st Military District, Commander Zivota Panic, concerning the way in which the siege of Vukovar was conducted.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, do I need to read what I wrote and then give the interpretation, or can it be seen on the screen? From my point of view, from the theoretical point of view, and that of the doctrine which doesn't date back only to the JNA time and the SFRY, but it dates back to the times before Christ. Sunsu [phoen] used to say that that the towns are not to be attacked. They are bypassed but not attacked, because a conflict in an urban environment always requires the use of greater number of troops. That is to say, that urban conflict makes it impossible to use all types of equipment. As Gavez [phoen] says, when one starts sabre rattling when one employs the entire force, then one needs sufficient space. Based on that, I think that the way Vukovar was liberated contradicts the theory and the doctrine. It is not consistent with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You've explained that and you've answered Mr. Borovic's question. You gave your own view, which is to say that in your opinion, this was a mistake committed by Zivota Panic and the command of the 1st Military District. I'm now approaching the final stages of my examination, and I would now like to turn to several of your conclusions. Can we please look at page 97. Paragraph 7, where you say that what took place, in a way, surprised the JNA which was partially unprepared for that type of war because it had been created on a different premise. And then you speak about the TO which existed in the republics which, at that time, was not lawful, was not permitted. Do you have any additional comments or do you believe that this was completely clear?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honour, precisely as I put it in paragraph 7, it is a fact that the system of All People's Defence and social self-protection in the then SFRY, if viewed from the perspective of armed forces, their place and role was primarily designed and oriented toward repelling an external aggression, as it is in fact stated here. One of the most important matters that was constantly being promoted was the brotherhood and unity of peoples. It is a fact that the Yugoslav Peoples' Army was manned by members of all peoples and minorities. The experience shows that once civil war breaks out in a country, the first to perish or the first to suffer are the armed forces because there, they start bursting at the seams.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In paragraph 9 of your conclusions, you speak of what you just mentioned, that the first task of the JNA was to separate the warring parties until, as you put it here, there broke out direct conflict with the Croatian paramilitary forces. You speak here of the lifting of the blockade of the barracks. I have two questions in relation to this. Generally speaking, the JNA barracks, in view of the JNA doctrine which was focused on external aggression could it have been easy to block the JNA barracks in view of the fact that we were predominantly positioned in towns? Would you have an assessment to make in that respect as to how it was possible for them to be imposed blockades?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the fact of the matter is that the barracks which housed the commands of units and other facilities of the JNA were blocked to different -- and were exposed to different degrees of fire-power. In one of such barracks in Zagreb, I, myself, was present, and that was the Centre of Technical Schools. The second matter I wanted to say was that none of the JNA facilities can abandon a certain location without receiving prior orders which means that those who happened to be in the barracks at the time were unable to leave the premises of their own accord. All the barracks present in a certain town were easy prey and could easily be blocked. The exercise did not require strong forces. Whoever wanted to impose a blockade on a barracks was able to do so in view of the strength of the forces present in the barracks. I don't know if I made myself sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You did. Thank you. The blockade of barracks also implied the cutting off of water, electricity, and other supplies. Was this easily done as well?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: I can speak from the experience I had in the barracks where I was. From the 15th of September, 1991, onwards, water, electricity, and phone lines were discontinued and we were not allowed to leave the barracks' perimeter. I cannot speak for other barracks, but I can assert that this was the case in the barracks where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Although you say you cannot speak about the other barracks but let us take the barracks in Belgrade -- in Bjelovar because it was quite a typical example. Do you know what happened to the barracks in Bjelovar, if you have any information to that effect? For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, Bjelovar is in Croatia, specifically in western Slavonia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Domazet, we were learning about what was happening in the barracks in Bjelovar based on what we heard over the radio and television. In view of the fact that I only have this information concerning the barracks, I would say that they do not allow me to objectively portray the situation as it was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Of course. I understand. Do you recall that that particular barracks surrendered to the forces surrounding it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: I believe that it was in Virovitica that the barracks was surrendered, if I am correct. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, I do not want to ask you about the facts you're not certain of. I thought you knew something about it. But let's speak briefly about paragraph 11. That's your comment concerning the fact that the state of war was not declared. This seems to be a sort of criticism of yours. Is it your view as an expert that the country should have declared a state of war, or am I mistaken? Although this was the impression I got from the text you wrote there.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Domazet, this was not my opinion, as you summarised it now, that there should have been a state of war declared. Rather, paragraph 11 as one of the conclusions of a general nature relates to the following: When a state of war is declared in a country, one knows that a completely different system of relationship ought to apply in that country. I said that the fact that a state of war was not declared is something that should not be drawn upon at all, that it was along those lines that I meant and not that a state of war should have been declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since you examined Operation Vukovar and the combat activities taking place there, do you have an assessment to make on the following matter: You did give an assessment about the number of officers and soldiers involved in the operation. Would you have an assessment to make about the strength concerning the 204th Vukovar Brigade, that's to say among the forces on the other side? Would you have an assessment of the strength of those forces?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the figures indicating the size of the forces engaged in Operations Group South can be found at page 71, paragraph 62 of my report. The figure was provided by deputy commander of the 1st Military District, General Stojanovic, if I'm not mistaken. Therefore, this was not my position as to the size of the force. Rather, this was a figure taken from strictly confidential number 1614-162 dated 16 of November, 1991, and the figure was given in that document by deputy commander of the 1st Military District. In view of this, it is quite difficult to speak of the strength of the 204th Vukovar Brigade of the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you well, this was the only source you used in presenting this figure. Since you examined the documentation you had, would it come as a surprise to you if I were to tell you that recently the Croatian government passed a decision whereby more than 7.000 decorations were given to members of the 204th Brigade which meant that the brigade was more than 7.000 strong. Would this figure come as a surprise to you as an expert who examined the matter?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I didn't hear about this and I didn't know that. But if you look at the JNA brigades, under the wartime establishment they had around 6.000 troops, so this wouldn't come as a surprise really to me, the 7.000 men from the 204th Brigade, but I would not be inclined to think that the -- this was the establishment unit strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In your expert report, you rightly concluded that in respect of some matters, orders and papers were missing, especially so concerning some important decisions and the operations log of the Guards Brigade and so on and so forth. Can you tell us how can this be, since under the rules, every officer was duty-bound to hand over all the notes, the official notes he made, and this was in particular true of the operations logs, and especially in view of the fact that we are dealing with an elite Guards Brigade here.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I feel quite uncomfortable at this time to have to assess how and why these documents went missing. This would constitute a speculation on my part and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. You don't have to answer. I have another question. We had, as part of the Prosecution case, an expert, Mr. Wheeler, who gave an assessment of what happened in Vukovar, including the casualties and damage, as well as the extent of the destruction of the town itself. This view was given also in terms of whether it went in favour of either sides and that this was a God's given thing for the Croats and for Franjo Tudjman. Do you have an opinion in that regard?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: I must admit that I am unfamiliar with the position you presented by Mr. Wheeler. I can therefore only assume which factors were taken into consideration by the said gentleman either in favour or against this particular view.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please look at page 10, paragraph 11 of the report where you speak of Article 7 of the Law on the Armed Forces of the SFRY. I believe you quote the text of the oath taken by the soldiers, and could you please slowly read out the text?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: "I, full name, take -- hereby pledge to defend the independence, constitutional order, inviolability and integrity of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and to protect and spread the brotherhood and nations and our nationalities. I shall always scrupulously and with discipline fulfill the obligations and responsibilities of a defender of my -- as a defender of my socialist self-managed homeland and be prepared without sparing my own life to fight for its freedom and honour."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You go on to speak of the significance of this oath and that it was even signed and so on and so forth. Does it follow from there something that many people discussed and that was the defending of the integrity or the -- rather, yes, the integrity of the territory of what was then SFRY?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: My answer can be yes, but it wasn't the task of the JNA alone. It was a task enshrined in the Law on the Armed Forces, which included the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. I think this might be a good time for the break, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing against that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at a quarter to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Forca.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: It is on behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin's Defence team that I will be asking you some questions about issues of interest to our Defence. The first thing I want to know is you were asked a question about the fact that the Guards Motorised Brigade was used in a way that was contrary to its purpose. What I want to know is what was the purpose of the Guards Motorised Brigade. Can you tell us that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, it wasn't my understanding, I didn't say contrary to its purpose, I would say contrary to its fundamental purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fundamental purpose.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: The fundamental basic purpose of the Guards Brigade was to protect important persons and buildings as well as a number of activities involving protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, was it not precisely because of the nature of its fundamental purpose that the structure of the Guards Brigade was different from the structure of other brigades, the alpine brigade, the mountain brigade and so on and so forth. At page 12 of the your report, you provide a chart of the structure of the Guards Brigade as it was when it was sent to Vukovar back in 1991 when there were units there that were attached. I want to know about the structure of the Guards Brigade. Was it any different before it was dispatched to Vukovar, so if I may term that in its peacetime structure.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, there are two questions there. First of all, was it structure any different from that of other brigades? The answer is yes. The other question at page 12 in paragraph 20, you have a description of how the Guards Brigade was organised at the time it was sent to Vukovar. It is stated that the security battalion which was part of the brigade was not sent there as specified by the order for the chief of the General Staff. The security battalion was not sent to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Under peacetime conditions, would the structure of the Guards Brigade have been different from any other kind of brigade, such as the alpine brigade, the mountain brigade, the infantry brigade, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When you wrote your expert report, did you bear in mind the Zagreb agreement on the evacuation of wounded and ill from the Vukovar Hospital which, as we heard here, was signed on the 18th of November, 1991? Did you look at that document too?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: The document known as the Zagreb agreement is a document that I took into account in the sense of not having come across -- I at least did not come across anything to indicate that this document was known to any of the commanders and komandirs from the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: But that wasn't my question. I wanted to know whether you are aware of the document? You are, fine. Bearing in mind the importance of the hospital evacuation, which is something that you address in your report, you have this document signed at such a high level, an order for the hospital to be evacuated in keeping with this agreement. Would that sort of thing not have to be provided in writing containing all the criteria and all the elements of the evacuation itself?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: In my reply, first of all, I wish to say something about the Zagreb agreement which is what Mr. Bulatovic is asking me about. As the Defence made available to me whatever they had at the time, I looked at the -- a lot of OTP expert evidence. Personally I did not realise that the Zagreb agreement was there. There was no copy of the Zagreb agreement that was included in my sets. Another thing I wish to say is any operation at that sort of level should, in my understanding, in my understanding of the way the system of command and control works, should be in writing or in a written form, the wording used by Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, you say that Tactical Group North and Operations Group South were supposed to be involved in concerted action to take the hospital. That was the operation. Bearing in mind what we've just said, would it not be logical for an order like that, I mean the evacuation order, precisely because of the involvement of both Tactical Group North and OG South to have been written by the command of the 1st Military District, would that not be a logical sequence of events in keeping with the rules and regulations that applied throughout the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: I must say I remember the order to take concerted action to achieve this. This was sent to OG South. It is hardly logical or against the rules for the specific order or an addendum of a previous decision to be written by the command of the 1st Military District. That would not be contrary to the system of command and control, it would not run counter to the system of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, based on the documents which you inspected and which you used in writing your report, and based on which you draw your conclusions, can you tell us whose zone of responsibility did the Ovcara farm fall under from the 18th of November onwards? It was the area of responsibility of which specific unit. Can you help with us that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: The way I see it as operations were unfolding within the framework of the Vukovar operation, and as the combat disposition was being shifted, the location of Ovcara, from the date you specify onwards -- just a minute please. Let me see if I have that. I mean it is a well-known fact that commands were designated, town commands, rather, for those parts of the area that were liberated or for those parts of the area that were within the general area covered by the ongoing operations. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, perhaps I could give you a hand. The question was very specific. You say that Operations Group South had its own area of responsibility so this is my question, just in order to clarify, and we can get to this later on. What about the units that are part of OG South, do they have their own area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: When we talked about the area assigned to an attacking unit, at the joint tactical level, such as the brigade or further up the chain, we talk about the operations area of that unit. Within that operations area of a tactical unit such as a battalion or an assault detachment, an axis is designated or assigned. The technical term is an axis of attack or a sector of attack, and that was also specified in the decision to attack a built-up area. Along that axis of attack of those units, yes, I suppose you could speak of their area of responsibility as referring to the area in which they carry out combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about what we find on page 83 of your report, paragraph 93 when you say that: "Command posts were established in the villages of Negoslavci, Berak, and Ovcara." And as stated in paragraph 98: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, based on the rules of command and control and in keeping with the relevant regulations, all what you've been saying about the structure of OG South, namely that in terms of the establishment, they were all brought up to the same level, Colonel Vojinovic, as the commander of the 80th Brigade, who does he take his orders from? You said the level was the same.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: The commander of the 80th Brigade, which within OG South was subordinate to the commander of OG South, can take orders from the commander of OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that the commander of the military police company of the 80th Brigade takes orders from his own superior, the brigade commander Vojinovic; is that not right, sir? Now, if we have the military police company commander of the 80th Brigade and someone gives him an order and this person giving the order is not a member of the superior command and is not his direct superior, what is the commander of the military police company to do, having received an order from someone who is not his superior?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: This is a matter of principle. It mustn't necessarily involve the commander of the military police company. As such, this applies to any commander or unit commander. There are two types of relationships in the army, the superior/subordinate relationship, which is a relationship of subordination; and the junior/senior relationship which normally implies a difference in rank or a difference in the time when a rank was awarded. At any rate, if any officer takes an assignment from a senior officer or a higher-ranking officer in relation to his own direct superior, this officer is duty-bound to first and foremost inform his direct superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And before informing his superior, must he carry out the order?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: He is duty-bound to tell the person issuing him the order that he must inform his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us go back to the town commands which are quite interesting to us. We're speaking specifically of Ovcara now. In your report, paragraph 98 says that in the war book of the 80th Motorised Brigade for the 19th of November, it is recorded that the order was that Captain First Class," I'm not going to mention his name, "was appointed commander of the village of Ovcara on the evening of the 19th of November." Now I'm now interested in the rules of service and legal regulations of the JNA. What are the powers of the town or village commander? You said that one set of rules applied to peacetime and one set of rules applied to wartime. I'm now focusing on the wartime situation.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I already spoke about this to a certain extent. In the orders issued on establishing the town command, there was a clause specifying that rules of service were to be complied with, namely the provisions pertaining to garrison and service in the barracks. The rules of service in those provisions that I just specified, meaning from Article 78 onwards, deal with garrisons and barracks, but not in wartime. In that respect, the order for everyone to draw the instructions on how to act as town commander there should be tasks very specifically defined as well as conduct and actions to be taken in a particular town as ordered by the town commander. Town or village commands are first and foremost in the disciplinary sense superior to everyone located in that town or village as they were, in my view, unable to effect the combat tasks received by the units stationed in that town or village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Forca, what can the town commander do in order to exercise his duty to ensure discipline?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Most likely it should have been regulated in relation to each particular town or village and the units stationed there were different. Commanders of battalions and artillery battalions functioned under different circumstances and their composition was different too. So it was a very diverse situation, and thus it's hard to say exactly what each of town commanders had available in order to implement their task unless it was specified in the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, in accordance with the roles of service in the armed forces, is it possible for someone uninvited, unannounced or any other term of that nature to come to the area of responsibility of a particular unit, and if that happens, what is the procedure? What must the commander of that unit do in relation to such unannounced, uninvited persons?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: In keeping with the orders on establishing town or village commands, there shouldn't be an occasion where somebody unannounced or uninvited comes to an area of responsibility. This is something that shouldn't happen, at least not deliberately. However, that doesn't mean that somebody uninvited, as you said, can come into the area of responsibility without being noticed by the person in charge. So there are two aspects there. If a person who was uninvited entered an area of responsibility, and if the commander of that town or village knew about that, then the person appointing him can take measures in relation to that town commander as specified by the regulations. If this uninvited, undesired person entered the area of responsibility without that being known to the commander, if this was, that is to say, a complete surprise to the commander then, logically speaking, one would need to establish who was responsible for this, for this uninvited person entering the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, I am interested in what a town commander can do in such a person, uninvited, unannounced person entering the area of responsibility. Do they send them away, do they inquire as to why, how, and for what purpose they have come? Do they ask for a report of the command to which this uninvited person was subordinated? That's what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honour, now, in a portion of my answer, I can speak both in hypothetical terms and in terms of the roles. In hypothetical terms, I never received any kind of instructions which town commands were duty-bound to write in compliance with the orders. On the other hand, there are rules which regulate the guard service and how they must treat persons who are either uninvited or undesired and enter the area. So these are the rules of the guard service which regulate how these persons are halted or apprehended and, in case that they respond to the order to halt, how they are to be treated. And likewise, how they are treated if they fail to respond to the call to halt.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Forca. We're not going to spend more time on this. I'm now interested in something else. In accordance with the rules and regulations applied in command and control of the armed forces, can a brigade commander send his subordinate officers or, rather, instruct his subordinate officers to receive their orders from some other officers who are not members of that establishment formation, establishment unit, and is there such a possibility envisaged in the regulations?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Forgive me, Mr. Bulatovic, can a brigade commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, can a brigade commander instruct his subordinate officer to receive an order from, say, a major who is a member of some other unit?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: In order to reply, I need to tell you something first. Within a brigade, there is a command system where the relations are defined. These relations within the command system may be linear; that is to say, commander of a brigade, commander of battalion, commander of battalion to the commander of company. This is the linear relation or the relation of subordination. The other type of relations are functional relations. Within functional relations, there is the staff of the brigade and commander of battalion, which is to say that commander of brigade is superior to the commander of battalion and only he can issue orders to him or the Chief of Staff in the absence of the commander. So this is as far as the functional relations are concerned. Battalion commander cannot receive orders from staff organs without prior authorisation from the brigade commander. The third type of relations that exist within the command and control system are staff relations. In staff relations, each command organ of the brigade has a staff relation with the brigade commander and the brigade commander has a linear relation with them. Now we're all speaking in hypothetical terms now. If, in the command and control system there are -- or, rather, there is a so-called principle of competence, this principle of competence means that when orders are issued, levels may not be skipped, which is to say that, in principle, when the situation does not so require, and only on rare circumstances will the brigade commander issue a task to a company commander if there exists a battalion commander. As I am saying, this is in principle, depending on the situation. Theoretically and practically, it is possible to expand the competence in issuing orders. What does this mean? The competence in issuing orders can be expanded in two cases. The first one is in relation to units and organs and competencies or authorities. For example, if, in an area, if in a captured territory there are several units from various establishment units, then one of them, usually the most senior one, will take over the command over those units, and this is how his competencies are expanded in relation to the organs of these units. The second case is this: If a unit receives an order to carry out an operation and competencies are specified for that operation, and in view of the commander the situation requires that another operation or task be carried out, then such a commander can have his competencies expanded. So this is the theory behind it. And in accordance with this --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: The brigade commander can, as you said, exempted or detached the company commander and sends him to another officer who is not his commander to receive an order from him. Now, for that to happen, the situation would have to be an extremely extraordinary one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Forca, once again, something to do with the roles. If the officers from superior command happen to come on some basis for an inspection or for some other purpose, they happen to come to subordinate units, can then any orders be issued by officers from subordinate command to these officers from superior command? Could you please answer this briefly?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: If I understood your question, a superior sent to the subordinate unit an inspection team and there arises a situation where members of the inspection team --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can the officer of the subordinate unit issue any order to those inspection team members?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: In principle, no. Because these officers who had come to conduct an inspection had to have authority granted to them by the commander as to what they were to inspect and what is covered by their inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, I'm now going to turn briefly to another topic and then I will be concluding my cross-examination -- or, rather, my examination. You were asked by Mr. Domazet about previous actions, and you said in your report that in order to understand the Vukovar operation, one had to know the processes and events in the SFRY that were taking place at the time and so on and so forth. I don't want to belabour the point and what was covered by Mr. Domazet and I will ask you something else. In your report, would you please find page 55, paragraph 18, where you speak about cease-fires signed between the Republic of Croatia and the Presidency of the SFRY or whoever was signing these cease-fires at the time. Apparently there was an agreement reached in The Hague on the 4th of October, 1991, on cease-fire until the 19th of October, 1991. Then there was a meeting between Lord Carrington and Hans Van den Broek, Franjo Tudjman, Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Kadijevic. The UN Security Council passed a resolution on the 25th of September, 1991, this is Resolution 713. Can you tell us how many times the cease-fire was violated, the cease-fire signed at these levels?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the cease-fires -- or, rather, the violations of the cease-fires mentioned on page 55, paragraph 18, were taken from the collection of documents and reprinted here, although these matters are also mentioned in the subsequent parts of the report where documents from the 1st Military District were mentioned as were those from the level of the SSNO. I cannot say how many cease-fires were reached exactly, but I believe that there were around 10 or at least we have -- and how many were violated. I know that the cease-fire signs were 14 but the violations were definitely more than 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many attacks on JNA installations and JNA troops took place in this period? I'm speaking about the period from the 4th of October to the 3rd of November.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes. Paragraph 18 does read that the paramilitary forces of Croatia carried out 247 attacks on JNA facilities and occupied five barracks and two military facilities. This is the report --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This is the period from early October up until -- or rather -- until the 19th of October? So that is the number?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes. In this mentioned period, from the 19th of October to the 3rd of November, there were 217 attacks on JNA units and facilities as stated in that document I mentioned on page 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, do you know that in the month of April there were attacks on JNA facilities? Specifically, do you know of the attack on the JNA military court during trial against Mr. Spegelj in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Zagreb at the time, but I am not familiar with details. I know that there was an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the instance where a JNA soldier was being strangled in Split?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I think that there are a few who have not seen the image of what you were referring to in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know or are you aware of the methods employed by the paramilitary forces of Croatia, the ZNG, HOS forces in arming themselves and the channels they used for the purpose?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Your Honours, in Exhibit 806, collection of documents, among other things the methods used for the illegal [Realtime transcript read in error "legal"] arming of the Croatian paramilitary army are indicated. Specifically, in paragraph 24 at page 56 this particular piece of information is to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If I can only intervene, on page 95, line 3, in the transcript, it reads "legal arming," and I was speaking of the illegal arming of the Croatian paramilitary army and of their paramilitary formations. Are you aware of the instant where a train carriage was intercepted on its way from Slovenia and the contents of the carriage, namely weapons, were seized by the Croatian paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes, I can say that I heard of the incident but I am not familiar with details. I can merely say that I heard of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Forca, I wasn't asking about any details. I merely wanted to know if you were aware of this, and when the time comes, we will deal with the other aspects of it. I'm interested in something else. Did you hear of Boeing 707, of the Bulgarian air company that the JNA air force planes forced to land on the Pleso airport in Zagreb? The plane was used for transporting weapons intended for the Croatian paramilitary forces, and the funds were collected through the Croatian National Fund in Toronto. Since you were in Zagreb at the time, are you familiar with this? And do you know that the Croatian paramilitary forces and the MUP forces fired upon the aircraft as it landed on the airport with the intention of destroying its -- the cargo it held?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with the incident, but I don't know whether the events really took place the way you said. The documents which I used and consulted do mention the plane that was popularly knowing as Kikas, or otherwise Boeing 707. I believe the public at large is aware of the incident, although I'm not familiar with the details you mentioned later on as to who opened fire on the plane and the details about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 23 of your expert report, you mention some details along those lines, not the ones that I mentioned, but you state that this was the transporting the weapons collected by Croatian businessmen and intellectuals in Toronto. There were 225 persons in all who were also members of the HDZ. Another matter that is contained in your expert report in paragraph 103, there it states that the evacuation of the hospital was also a problem in terms of security. Does this mean that security organs had to be present during the evacuation of the hospital in order to exercise their powers as defined by the legislation that was in force at the time? And I do not wish to go into the specific pieces of legislation.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes, the paragraph does read the way you put it that, in my view, the evacuation of the hospital was also a security problem and of course since it was a security problem, the security organs had to be involved in the operation with the authorities that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Forca, in 1991 at the time of these events, who was the president of the SFRY Presidency, or was it Mr. Stipe Mesic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes, I presumed that this was your question. After several attempts, he was elected president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And he was the president until the 12th of December, 1991. Do you know what his statement before the Croatian parliament was upon the expiry of his term of office as president of the Presidency? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: I wouldn't dare speak of his statement in any certain terms. In other words, I don't know exactly what his statement was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If you do not, no matter. It was broadcast and reported on, but the statement was that he had accomplished his task, that Yugoslavia was no more. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR FORCA
utterances.text: Yes, along those lines, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, that was effective, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's approximately 20 minutes to go. Could we break today and start tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. How long would you hope to anticipate?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I hope to finish within the second session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Within the second session, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to go all day tomorrow. It would be convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It would be convenient if we started at 9.30 tomorrow, but that shouldn't interfere with your ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That would be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. I think this is the third time recently we've done this, so it's probably most people now have had the benefit of it. We will adjourn now. We will resume tomorrow at 9.30 and we will finish the witness by no later than 1.45 tomorrow. And that should leave you at least the last session, Mr. Borovic, given Mr. Weiner's anticipation -- Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 19th day of October, 2006, at 9.30 a.m.
